newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's CSS defends oil component of PPI data.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's CSS defends oil component of PPI data.

text.p: South Africa's Central Statistical Service (CSS) on Wednesday defended the way it calculates the crude oil component of the producer price index after criticism by economists of the latest data.
The argument centres on the "other minerals component" of the PPI data, which is largely made up of crude oil prices and has a 4.33 percent weighting in the overall index.

Economists asked why this component rose 0.1 percent month- on-month in July and fell by 0.6 percent in August and 1.4 percent in September, despite a 6.5 percent rise in the rand oil price in July and a further 9.0 percent rise in August and September.
In a statement, CSS head Mark Orkin said the service received detailed basic information on the quantity and total price of imported crude petroleum from Customs and Excise (C&E) on a monthly basis.
"The weighted average unit price is then calculated and anomalies are checked with C&E," he said. "In the past errors have been found and corrected."
He said Customs and Excise were reluctant for the CSS to reveal the basic information.
"However, the CSS can report that the calculated unit prices reflect monthly changes of +0.5 percent for July, -2.0 percent for August and -2.2 percent for September 1996.

"The weight of imported crude petroleum crude petroleum in the PPI is 1.75 percent, which means that for it to have an effect of 0.1 percent on the PPI, the unit price will have to increase by 5.7 percent."
Orkin said the landed cost of crude, derived from C&E data, was reflected in the imported component of the PPI.
"There is a completely different price, the In Bond Landed Cost of final products. This affects the manufacturing part of the PPI through the refinery price of petrol, diesel and paraffin."
He said the weight of these products in the total PPI was 3.48 percent.

"The CSS gets these prices directly from the refineries. The calculated price index for these products reflects monthly changes of -1.8 percent for July, +0.2 percent for August and +1.8 percent for September 1996."
"For me there is nothing left to be mysterious about," he told Reuters.
"(The statement) does not tell us anything except that if there is a problem with the figures, that it lies with Customs and Excise. That is all that this really says," one said.
"While I understand that the landed cost of crude is not precisely the same as converting the Brent price into rand, they should move in the same way," she added.

Transnet economist Mike Schussler agreed. "I think their crude price is wrong...there is no doubt in my mind about that and it could be substantially wrong. And if it is substantially wrong then it could have a substantial influence (on the component)," he said.
Overall PPI rose 7.6 percent year-on-year and 0.4 percent month-on-month in September.
